name: Google Cloud Storage
summary: Google Cloud’s object storage, where even the archive class answers in milliseconds.
intro: Cloud Storage keeps objects in buckets, and each bucket lives in a location you pick: one region (copies across zones), a dual-region pair, or a multi-region such as `US` or `EU`. Writes, reads after writes and listings are strongly consistent everywhere, so a successful upload is visible to the next request. Objects can be up to 5 TiB.

Each object has a storage class: Standard, Nearline, Coldline or Archive. The colder classes cost less to store but add retrieval fees and minimum storage periods of 30, 90 and 365 days. Unlike S3 Glacier or Azure’s archive tier, every class serves data in milliseconds, with no restore step. Autoclass can move objects for you: an object unread for 30 days drops to Nearline, and reading it moves it back to Standard.
strengths: Archive data is readable immediately, with no hours-long rehydration
Strong global consistency for writes, overwrites and listings
Dual-region and multi-region buckets, with optional turbo replication that copies new data to the second region within 15 minutes
Autoclass handles tiering by access pattern, so you don’t write lifecycle rules
limits: Each object name can be written about once per second; faster updates to the same object get throttled
Nearline, Coldline and Archive charge retrieval fees and bill for 30, 90 or 365 days even if you delete earlier
Its native JSON API is its own; S3 tools work only through the XML API with HMAC keys, and not every feature maps

snippet.title: Create an Autoclass bucket, upload, and notify Pub/Sub on new objects
source: # publish a Pub/Sub message every time an object is written
gcloud storage buckets notifications create gs://acme-media \

story: Four years after Amazon launched S3, Google opened a storage service of its own to outside developers. Announced on 19 May 2010, at Google I/O, as Google Storage for Developers, it was a RESTful service replicated across several US data centres, with `gsutil`, an open-source command-line tool, for managing it. The preview was open to a limited number of developers from a waiting list, each with up to 100 GB of storage and 300 GB of monthly bandwidth free. It opened to all developers, with no invitation needed, in May 2011, and was later renamed Google Cloud Storage. Today it runs on Colossus, Google’s cluster file system and the successor to the Google File System (GFS).

Its distinctive bet was that cold data shouldn’t mean slow data. Nearline launched in 2015 with retrieval in about three seconds; today it, Coldline (2016) and Archive (2020) all use the same API as Standard and answer in milliseconds. Instead of waiting hours for a restore, as with S3 Glacier or Azure’s archive tier, you pay a retrieval fee and a minimum storage period. Archive launched in January 2020 at $0.0012 per GB-month, with tape replacement as a headline use.
Location became the other lever: Regional and Multi-Regional classes in 2016, and in 2026 Rapid buckets that place objects in a single zone next to the compute that reads them.

choices.choice: Every storage class answers in milliseconds
choices.why: Google wanted archived data usable without changing applications. As it put it when Coldline launched, existing systems could store and access cold data “without any updates to the application”.

choices.choice: Built on Google’s internal file system
choices.why: Rather than a separate stack, Cloud Storage sits on Colossus, the same storage layer that backs Firestore and other Google services.
Multi-region buckets keep serving through a regional outage, regional ones sit next to compute, and zonal Rapid buckets trade redundancy for speed. You pick per bucket, not per account.

choices.choice: An S3-style XML API beside its own JSON API
choices.why: Supporting HMAC keys and an XML API close to S3’s lets many tools written for S3 work against Cloud Storage by changing the endpoint.

timeline.text: Announced as Google Storage for Developers at Google I/O; limited preview (May)
Opens to all developers, with objects up to 5 TB (May)
Nearline class for rarely read data, still online (March)
Coldline, plus Multi-Regional and Regional classes (October)
Archive class at $0.0012 per GB-month, readable in milliseconds (January)
Rapid buckets store objects in one zone beside compute (March)
